catalog_quote: ダグール語のアクセントは一定の型を有していていかなる対立も示さず，したがって音韻論的には無意味である。そのため従来の記述も一般にきわめて簡略で，Pは常に第一音節が強いとし (P. p. 126)，Zはこれに加えて第二音節以下に長母音があればそこが高いとする (Z. p. 13) のみである。... いずれにせよ筆者のみるところでは，強さよりもむしろ高さがアクセントの主体をなしており，しかも特に高さに関しては音節よりモーラ単位でとらえるほうが正確で簡潔な記述ができる。それによれば，強めは原則として第一モーラにあり，高さの山はうしろから二番目のモーラ（ただしそこが副モーラにあたるときはその直前の主モーラ）にあるとすれば済む。 [English summary pp. 239-240:] If we admit a time-based unit 'mora', which takes the form of either (1) a syllable-initial (C)(S)V or (2) a postvocalic V or a syllable-final C, we can say that all the shortest words in Dagur consist of two moras. In terms of this unit, the non-phonemic accent in Dagur is generalized as follows: the stress, in principle, falls on the first mora, and the penultimate mora has the highest pitch; if the penultimate mora is the non-initial type (i.e. type (2) above), the preceding syllable-initial mora will be pronounced the highest. new_statements.quote: ダグール語のアクセントは一定の型を有していていかなる対立も示さず，したがって音韻論的には無意味である。そのため従来の記述も一般にきわめて簡略で，Pは常に第一音節が強いとし (P. p. 126)，Zはこれに加えて第二音節以下に長母音があればそこが高いとする (Z. p. 13) のみである。[…] いずれにせよ筆者のみるところでは，強さよりもむしろ高さがアクセントの主体をなしており，しかも特に高さに関しては音節よりモーラ単位でとらえるほうが正確で簡潔な記述ができる。それによれば，強めは原則として第一モーラにあり，高さの山はうしろから二番目のモーラ（ただしそこが副モーラにあたるときはその直前の主モーラ）にあるとすれば済む。
new_statements.translation: Dagur accent has a fixed pattern and shows no oppositions whatsoever, so it is phonologically irrelevant. For that reason earlier descriptions are generally very brief: P[oppe 1930] says the first syllable is always strong (p. 126), and Z[hong 1982] only adds that if there is a long vowel in the second or a later syllable, that syllable is high (p. 13). [...] In any case, as I see it, pitch rather than intensity forms the main substance of the accent, and pitch in particular can be described more accurately and simply in terms of morae than syllables. On that basis it suffices to say that the intensity peak lies in principle on the first mora and the pitch peak on the second mora from the end (or, when that is a secondary mora, on the main mora immediately before it).

The English summary on pp. 239-240 (view/) reads exactly: 'In terms of this unit, the non-phonemic accent in Dagur is generalized as follows: the stress, in principle, falls on the first mora, and the penultimate mora has the highest pitch; if the penultimate mora is…
new_statements.translation_language: Japanese (author's own English summary p. 239-240: 'the non-phonemic accent in Dagur is generalized as follows: the stress, in principle, falls on the first mora, and the penultimate mora has the highest pitch; if the penultimate mora is the non-initial type ..., the preceding syllable-initial mora will be pronounced the highest.')
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is non-contrastive. Dynamic stress (intensity) falls on the first syllable/first mora of the word (Poppe 1930 p.126 'always on the first syllable, even if its vowel is short and all later vowels long'; Poppe 1934 p.206; Nugteren 2011; Kuribayashi 1989 and Engkebatu 1988 as reported), while a separate pitch peak falls late in the word: on the penultimate mora (Tsumagari 1985, endorsed by Yamada 2020), described by others as the final syllable (Engkebatu 1988, Tsumagari 2003 per Ōtake 2012) or a non-initial long vowel (Zhong 1982). Martin 1961 instead treats word/phrase stress as predictable from vowel 'strength' (long/multiple vowels and a > o > i > u > e), conflating pitch and intensity according to Tsumagari.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; Martin 1961 marks 'secondary or weak stress' vs primary stress in his phrase-shape chart but gives no positional rule. The pitch peak (penultimate mora) is a second, independent prominence, not a secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Tsumagari: if the penultimate mora is a secondary mora (post-vocalic V or coda C) the pitch peak falls on the preceding main (CV) mora; fn.17: in short words the pitch peak can be hard to hear because of the first-mora intensity. Yamada 2020: the forward shift off a secondary mora is a tendency, some words keep the peak (ant, aul, ort vs bait, weil). Ōtake 2012: Chinese loans take native pitch pattern regardless of tone. Martin: free variation in relative vowel strength (e vs i,u).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms from a single Hailar-dialect speaker (Tsumagari); Martin 1961 says stress is phonemic only at sentence/phrase level and predictable within words. Non-first-syllable short vowels reduce to /i, ə, u/ (Tsumagari) — consistent with initial prominence. Reading 'fixed-initial' refers to the stress (intensity) component; the author himself regards the penultimate-mora pitch peak as the main exponent of 'accent', so a pitch-based coder could read fixed-penult(mora)/final.
new_statements.identity_note: Tsumagari 1985 describes the Hailar dialect (one speaker recorded in Japan); Poppe 1930/1934 also describe Hailar-area Dagur; Martin 1961 is based on the speech of Peter (Urgunge) Onon; Todaeva 1986 describes the Butkha dialect; Yamada 2020 uses Hailar, Butkha and Qiqihar consultants; Ōtake 2012 is an atypical Hohhot-raised idiolect. All fall under language-level daur1238; the initial-stress statement is consistent across Hailar (Poppe, Tsumagari) and the Butkha-based standard (Engkebatu 1988 as reported).

sources.locator: §3.2 アクセント, p. 237; English summary pp. 239-240
sources.note: §3.2 アクセント p. 237: accent has a fixed pattern, shows no oppositions, phonologically irrelevant; pitch rather than intensity is the main exponent; intensity ('強め') in principle on the first mora, pitch peak on the penultimate mora (or the preceding main mora if the penult mora is a secondary mora). English summary pp. 239-240: 'the stress, in principle, falls on the first mora, and the penultimate mora has the highest pitch'. Reviews Poppe 1930 p.126 (first syllable always strong), Zhong 1982 p.13 (plus non-initial long vowel is high), Martin 1961 pp.4-15.

sources.note: pp. 4-5 §1.1-1.2: stress is phonemic only at sentence level (one sentence stress, one phrase stress per phonological phrase); within phrases or words its location is predictable from the shape of the word/phrase in terms of relative vowel 'strength' (VV/VVV sequences dominate single vowels; strength order a, o, i, u, e, n), with a chart of phrase-shape types; upper/lower case marks primary vs weak stress throughout. Not a simple positional rule.

sources.note: p. 126 §12 'Ударение': stress is expiratory and always on the first syllable, even when its vowel is short and all following vowels are long (Hailar-area Dagur).

sources.citation: Yamada, Yōhei 山田洋平. 2020. ダグール語の述部の諸相 [Aspects of the predicate in Dagur]. PhD dissertation, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. doi:10.15026/94834.
sources.note: §1.3.3.5 アクセント pp. 30-32 (data mainly Hailar and Qiqihar speakers): no position-contrastive accent; each word has an intensity peak and a pitch peak; Kuribayashi 1989 puts stress always on the first syllable, Zhong 1982 adds that a non-initial long vowel is pronounced high; endorses Tsumagari 1985's summary (intensity on first mora, pitch peak on penultimate mora) with own examples and a note that the pitch peak tends to, but need not, shift forward off a secondary mora.

sources.citation: Ōtake, Masami 大竹昌巳. 2012. ダグール語の音韻 ―共時的記述と通時的記述― [Dagur phonology: synchronic and diachronic description]. 地球研言語記述論集 4: 13-44. Kyoto: RIHN Indus Project.
sources.note: §2.2.4 韻律: accent has no distinctive function but a fixed pattern; describes pitch (acute-marked peaks, mostly on the last syllable) for an idiolect of a Hohhot-raised speaker ('X dialect', Mongolian-influenced); fn.10: per Tsumagari 1985: 237f, Engkebatu 1988: 149f, Tsumagari 2003: 135, pitch and stress are independent and stress is placed on the first syllable; per Engkebatu 1988: 150 and Tsumagari 2003: 135 pitch is prominent on the final syllable.
